(This evening through Tuesday)...
Issued at 211 PM EDT Tue Sep 15 2026

Overview.

After a stormy night tonight, hot and humid conditions will peak on 
Wednesday before a slow-moving front brings additional showers and 
thunderstorms to Central Indiana. Outside of a strong wind gust in 
the strongest storms of the day, the main threat will be localized 
heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Rain chances will linger into 
Thursday as the front becomes quasi-stationary over the area. 
Another stronger cold front will push through late this weekend into 
early next week bringing additional rain and cooler temperatures.

Tonight Through Thursday.

Rain coverage is expected to gradually ramp up during the evening 
and early overnight hours as a front approaches from the west and 
interacts with a hot and humid airmass over the state. The CAPE 
profile will be skinny, but deep peaking in the mid-adternoon hours 
at around 1500 J/kg. During the overnight hours, convection is 
expected to be elevated and driven more by frontal lift. Overall, 
the severe threat looks minimal with the weak instability profile 
and elevated nature of the storms, but with 30-40kts of shear as the 
LLJ ramps up, can't rule out a storm overperforming. The main threat 
looks to be localized heavy rain with the HREF max showing pockets 
of 2-2.5 inches in spots. Overall, most areas will see generally a 
half inch or less, but those localized areas could see minor 
flooding.

Another hot and humid day is expected for Wednesday with a much 
more saturated vertical profile in the aftermath of the storms 
Tuesday night. Surface dew points will be in the low to mid 70s with 
highs topping out in the upper 80s to low 90s. Convective debris may 
limit the higher-end temperature threat, but will have to monitor. 
With peak heat index values generally in the upper 90s to low 100s, 
not expecting a need for a Heat Advisory at this time, especially 
considering the potential for cooler spots due to convection and 
clouds.

As a quasi-stationary baroclinic zone sags into northern and central 
portions of the state Wednesday afternoon, shortwave energy embedded 
in zonal flow aloft will interact with a highly unstable airmass. 
Sounding profiles from the HRRR show SBCAPE values expanding to 1500-
2000 J/kg by mid-afternoon but shear looks fairly minimal at 15-
25kts. Additional showers and storms look likely throughout the day 
as the front remains in the area.Warm cloud depths exceeding 4000 
meters and boundary-parallel mean flow vectors favor high 
precipitation efficiency and potential training cells, which may 
allow for additional localized heavy rain and flash flooding. 

The surface front will slowly push southward across Southern Indiana 
on Thursday and become somewhat less pronounced as the main upper 
shortwave exits into the Great Lakes. While the loss of strongest 
PVA and a weakening LLJ will reduce overall convective intensity, 
lingering mid-level moisture and surface convergence along the 
boundary will maintain high shower and thunderstorm coverage through 
Thursday afternoon before post-frontal drying initiates Thursday 
night.

Friday Through Tuesday.

Generally hot and humid conditions are expected again Friday into 
the early weekend with the jet stream further north towards the 
Great Lakes and broad ridging across much of the Gulf states. There 
is some uncertainty as to any lingering impacts of the front from 
earlier in the week with some potential for a fairly sharp 
temperature gradient across the forecast area with the cooler air to 
the north and the warmer Gulf air to the south. Overall confidence 
is low with many details uncertain as to where the front will settle 
out.

A broader synoptic pattern shift takes hold towards the late weekend 
as operational GFS and ECMWF guidance, supported by GEFS and EPS 
ensemble means, drive a deepening mid-level trough across the Upper 
Midwest and Northeast. This front will bring additional showers and 
storms Sunday into Monday along with cooler weather to start the 
work week.
